doc.title: Jean Bach interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: John Kirby's band at the Pump Room
summary: The Kirby sextet's white-tie style, its personnel, and the O'Neil Spencer story at the hotel.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Yeah. It’s terrible. So I guess I did all my listening on their turf. Well, no, oh, John Kirby’s band played in the Pump Room of the Ambassador East Hotel, which was then the toniest hotel in Chicago. Beautiful. And the room was exquisite, with dark blue walls and white woodwork, and sconces and it was very stylish. And they’d had a lot of good bands in there — Teddy Wilson was there and at any rate, when Kirby played, they looked so marvelous. They had tail suits, full dress suits, but everything was in white. White tie and white tail suits and everything. The cast was Russell Procope on saxophone and Buster Bailey on clarinet. Billy Kyle was the piano player, and Charlie Shavers wrote the arrangements and played trumpet, and Kirby was the bassist. The drummer was a man named O’Neil Spencer, who also sang. So one day somebody checked in the hotel. It’d been in the papers, her name was Edith Rodgers Dahl and her husband, Whitey Dahl had been a flyer and was shot down by Franco it was during the war in Spain, and was in prison. And so she had sent a picture of herself. She was some tootsie with blonde hair, she played the violin in vaudeville. She sent a picture of herself to Franco and that was in all the papers. She was trying to get him out of prison. Meanwhile, O’Neil was apprehended on the stairs, I think coming from her room or going up to her room. And they said, “what are you doing?” He said, “I’m Miss Dahl’s arranger.” And they roared with laughter. They said, “this man can’t read music.” It was quick thinking. So there was a lot of sneaking around the stairs I guess in those days.
